sections.h2: What kind of place is Jersey County, Illinois, for a home seller?
sections.html:
Jersey County is a river county north of St. Louis, bounded by the Mississippi on the south, the Illinois River on the west and Macoupin Creek to the northwest. It was formed from Greene County on February 28, 1839, and Jerseyville is its seat and largest community. The Romanesque Revival courthouse there, finished in limestone cut at Grafton, had its cornerstone laid on July 4, 1893.

The county has 369 square miles of land and lies inside the St. Louis metro area. Many residents commute out of the county, and Census QuickFacts puts mean travel time to work at 27.1 minutes. Roads include U.S. 67 and Illinois routes 3, 16, 100, 109, 111 and 267. Pere Marquette State Park near Grafton and Principia College near Elsah anchor the river end of the county.

Most of the county sits in Jersey Community Unit School District 100, with smaller parts in Southwestern District 9, Alton District 11 and Greenfield District 10. Look up your parcel number first, because township, school district and floodplain status all follow the parcel.

sections.h2: What do Census figures show about Jersey County homes?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau estimates 21,160 residents for July 2025, down 1.7 percent from the 2020 base. Of the 7,965 households, 80.5 percent are owner-occupied, and the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $171,900. Median household income is $80,361, and the county issued 39 building permits in 2025.

About 24.2 percent of residents are 65 or older. That matters for tax relief, since the Assessor's office helps seniors prepare the senior homestead exemption and assessment freeze applications.

sections.h2: Which Jersey County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
The Treasurer, the Supervisor of Assessments, the Board of Review and the Code Administrator all work from the Government Building at 200 North Lafayette in Jerseyville, and all post weekday hours of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. The County Clerk answers rate questions and receives redeemed tax.

Jersey County offices a seller may need (source: Jersey County government website)

TreasurerSuite 5, (618) 498-5571 ext. 109, 110 or 111Billing, collection, delinquent tax

The Assessor's page also lists township assessors: one serves Jersey, Fidelity and Ruyle townships together, and another serves Mississippi Township. Since township assessors get the first look at an assessment, call yours before you file anything.

sections.h2: How is Jersey County real estate tax billed and paid?
sections.html:
The Treasurer's page says real estate tax is always a year behind when billed, while mobile home tax is for the current year. Due dates differ from year to year, so ask the office for the calendar covering your closing date. Interest is charged on anything paid after a due date, and state law sets that interest at 1 1/2 percent per month or part of a month in counties of this size (35 ILCS 200/21-15).

You have these ways to pay:

  • Online at jerseycountytax.com, where transaction fees apply.
  • Any of five Jerseyville banks, up to the due date only: Farmers State Bank, Heartland Bank & Trust, Jersey State Bank, Jerseyville Banking Center and Royal Banks.
  • The Treasurer's office or by mail once a bill is delinquent.
  • Mobile home tax, which can be paid only at the Treasurer's office or by mail.

A second property tax site, jerseyil.devnetwedge.com, is linked from the county pages for parcel inquiries.

sections.h2: What happens at the Jersey County tax sale?
sections.html:
The sale takes place in the auditorium of the Government Building. Only the delinquent taxes are sold, not the property itself. Once taxes are sold they must be redeemed through the County Clerk's office. If the taxes stay delinquent for 3 years, the Treasurer's page says the tax buyer can petition the court for a tax deed, and the statute on the period of redemption carries exceptions that depend on the property's status on the sale date (35 ILCS 200/21-350).

For a seller, the practical step is to ask the County Clerk for a redemption figure before you list, since sold tax has to be redeemed there.

sections.h2: How do I contest an assessment in Jersey County?
sections.html:
Begin with your township assessor, who has the first chance to change a value. If you cannot agree, ask the Board of Review for a hearing. The Board has three appointed members and hears complaints on value or exempt status for homes, businesses, condominiums and vacant land. It does not control the tax dollar amount, and a complaint about the bill itself is not a valid complaint.

Complaints are due within 30 days of newspaper publication of the assessment list (35 ILCS 200/16-55). For the 2025 changes, the county posted an appeal deadline of April 20, 2026, and that date has passed. Bring evidence to the hearing:

  • An exterior photo of your property and photos of at least three similar properties in your neighborhood.
  • Your property record card and the cards of comparable homes with lower assessments.
  • A recent appraisal, sales contract, settlement statement or deed, if you have one.

The Board mails its ruling. If you disagree, you may go to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board within 30 days of the decision notice (35 ILCS 200/16-160). The Assessor's forms page carries the Non-Farm Complaint (PTAX-230) and the Farm Complaint (PTAX-227).

sections.h2: Which exemption forms does the Jersey County Assessor offer?
sections.html:
The county's documents page lists applications by number, and the Assessor's office helps seniors prepare theirs. Ask the office for current dollar limits, because the county page names forms rather than amounts.

  • PTAX-329 and PTAX-340: senior citizens homestead exemption and assessment freeze, with separate 2025 and 2026 versions posted.
  • PTAX-343 and PTAX-343R: disabled person's homestead, initial and renewal.
  • PTAX-342 and PTAX-342R: standard homestead for disabled veterans.
  • PTAX-341: returning veterans.
  • PTAX-323: homestead improvement.
  • PTAX-245: disaster area reassessment.

For a house that was damaged, the disaster form may matter before you sell.

sections.h2: Do floodplain and permit rules affect selling a house in Jersey County?
sections.html:
They can. The Code Administration office reviews plans, issues building, storm water and floodplain permits, inspects new or substantially altered construction, and keeps elevation certificates for unincorporated Jersey County. It also keeps records of substantial improvements or damage to structures in the floodplain and investigates complaints under the International Property Maintenance Code.

Before listing a river-side or low-lying home, ask that office whether the parcel is in a mapped floodplain, whether any permit was left open, and whether a substantial-damage record exists. Manufactured homes fall under a county mobile home ordinance, and the Assessor's housing page links the state installation rules.

faqs.q: When is Jersey County property tax due?
faqs.a: The county says due dates differ from year to year and that real estate tax is billed a year behind. Ask the Treasurer at (618) 498-5571 for the dates tied to your closing.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Jersey County property tax in person?
faqs.a: Real estate tax can be paid at five Jerseyville banks until the due date. After that, pay at the Treasurer's office in the Government Building at 200 North Lafayette, Suite 5.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Jersey County assessment after the deadline?
faqs.a: The Board of Review handles complaints within 30 days of publication, so a missed window means waiting for the next assessment list. The posted date for the 2025 changes was April 20, 2026.

faqs.q: Does the Board of Review lower my tax bill?
faqs.a: No. It reviews assessed value only. The page says the tax dollar amount is not a valid complaint, and rate questions go to the County Clerk.

faqs.q: What is the fastest way to find out if my Jersey County parcel has tax sold?
faqs.a: Look up the parcel on the county's online tax site or call the Treasurer. If taxes were sold, redemption is made at the County Clerk's office.
